title: Things to do in Mauritius, region by region
summary: Places to see and things to do in the north, Port Louis, the centre, the east, the south, the west and south-west, and on Rodrigues. Each place has a line on what it is and what one does there, taken from the tourism promotion authority or from the place's own official page. Opening hours and entry fees are given only where such a page states them. Read on 20 November 2026.
audience: Visitors planning their days on the island, and the hosts, drivers and guides who advise them.

facts.label: National parks on land
facts.detail: Black River Gorges, proclaimed in 1994, and Bras d'Eau, proclaimed in 2011. Eight islets are national parks as well.

facts.label: Black River Gorges National Park
facts.detail: It holds the highest point of the island, at 828 metres.

facts.label: UNESCO World Heritage Sites
facts.detail: Aapravasi Ghat in Port Louis and Le Morne Cultural Landscape in the south-west.

facts.label: Proclaimed public beaches
facts.detail: Beach Authority lists dated 18 July 2025 and 14 January 2022.

facts.label: Offshore islets
facts.detail: Some are nature reserves or national parks.

facts.label: Aapravasi Ghat
facts.detail: Monday to Friday 9:00 to 16:00, Saturday 9:00 to 12:00. Closed on Sundays and public holidays.

facts.label: Rodrigues
facts.detail: The island is 18 km long and 8 km at its widest.

blocks.text: The Mauritius Tourism Promotion Authority divides the island into the north, Port Louis, the centre, the east, the south and the west. This guide follows that map and adds the south-west around Chamarel and Le Morne, and the island of Rodrigues. Everything on the island is within easy reach: it is about 61 km from north to south and 45 km from east to west.

Hours and fees change. Each one here is as the place's own page showed it on 20 November 2026. Fees quoted are those for visitors who are not residents of Mauritius. Many places charge residents less.

The north is the liveliest part of the island, centred on Grand Baie. It has shops and markets, restaurants and nightlife, sandy beaches with views of the northern islands, and old estates and temples inland.

items: Grand Baie. A village on a sheltered, horseshoe-shaped bay. You come for the shops, the cafés and restaurants along the bay, and live music and nightclubs in the evening.
Mont Choisy beach. A long curve of white sand around a bay, fringed by casuarina trees. You swim, snorkel and try watersports in the calm lagoon.
Trou aux Biches beach. A beach beside the town of the same name. You snorkel or dive, walk in the shade of the casuarinas and watch the sunset.

Cap Malheureux church. The red-roofed church of Notre Dame Auxiliatrice, in a fishing village on the northern tip. Visitors may go in, to join mass or to see the holy water basin made from a giant clam shell.

Maheswarnath Mandir, Triolet. A Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Shiva, founded in 1888 and described by the tourism authority as the largest on the island. You visit to see its pillars, sculptures and smaller temples.
Coin de Mire. An offshore island and protected nature reserve, reached by speedboat or catamaran. Landing is not allowed, so one watches the seabirds from the boat and snorkels or dives around it.
Ilot Gabriel. A small island with a white sandbar, reached by boat or catamaran from Grand Baie or Pereybère, for a day on the sand and in calm water.
Ile Plate, or Flat Island. An uninhabited island that was a quarantine station from the mid-19th century to the 1930s and still has a lighthouse. Divers visit the Shark Pit nearby.
Round Island and Serpent Island. Nature reserves where landing is not permitted. They are seen from the sea.

Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Botanic Garden, Pamplemousses. A garden of 33 hectares with 823 plant species, among them 80 palms. You walk its avenues to the pond of giant Amazon water lilies and the lotus ponds, alone or with an authorised guide.
L'Aventure du Sucre, Beau Plan. A museum in a former sugar mill, right next to the botanic garden. You follow the story of sugar in Mauritius and end with a tasting of sugars and rums.
Château de Labourdonnais, Mapou. A restored 19th-century mansion and its gardens. You tour the house, taste the estate's rums and fruit juices and visit the small animal farm.

blocks.text: Port Louis is the capital, in the north-west. Its centre is easy to walk: Le Caudan Waterfront, the Central Market, Aapravasi Ghat and Chinatown are within walking distance of each other. Its places of worship reflect the island's many cultures: the Jummah Masjid mosque, St Louis Cathedral, the Kwan Tee Pagoda and the Sockalingum Meenatchee Ammen Kovil temple.

items: Aapravasi Ghat World Heritage Site. The remains of the Immigration Depot built in 1849, where indentured labourers landed. You visit the Beekrumsing Ramlallah Interpretation Centre, then the depot itself. The whole visit takes about an hour.
La Citadel, or Fort Adelaide. A stone fort built by the British on a hill between 1830 and 1840. You go up for the view over the city.
Champ de Mars. A racecourse in the centre of the city, inaugurated in 1812. You go for a day at the races between late March and early December.
Kwan Tee Pagoda, Les Salines. A pagoda built by the Chinese community in 1842. Visitors step inside and walk in its gardens.

Blue Penny Museum, Le Caudan Waterfront. An art and history museum of Mauritius that holds the island's Post Office stamps. You walk through rooms on navigation, colonial history, old Port Louis and the post.
Natural History Museum, Chaussée. Four galleries on the wildlife, sea life and geology of the island, with a model and a skeleton of the dodo.
Odysseo Oceanarium, Les Salines. An indoor oceanarium of Indian Ocean species. You walk through at your own pace, with an audio guide if you rent one, and watch the feeding sessions.
Central Market. The market in the heart of the capital where local people buy fruit and vegetables. You walk the stalls, eat street food such as dholl puri and look for crafts on the first floor.
Le Caudan Waterfront. Shops, restaurants, a food court, a cinema and the Caudan Arts Centre beside the harbour, along a walkway hung with coloured umbrellas.
Chinatown. Narrow streets of old family shops close to the market. You eat biscuits, Chinese cakes and dim sum, and look at the murals on Royal Road, Emmanuel Anquetil Street and Venpin Street.

blocks.text: Inland there are mountains, old mansions and shopping malls. The Metro Express links Port Louis with Curepipe in the centre.

items: Trou aux Cerfs, Curepipe. The crater of a dormant volcano, 605 metres above sea level, with a small lake at its centre. You walk around it for the view.
Eureka House, Moka. A mansion from around 1836, now a museum, with 109 doors and windows. You take a guided tour, eat at the restaurant and walk in the gardens.
Domaine des Aubineaux, Curepipe. A colonial house built in 1872 where one can have lunch. It is one of the three estates of the Tea Route.
Le Pouce. A mountain of 812 metres, the third highest on the island. A marked trail leads to the top and back in three to four hours, with a view over Port Louis.

Pieter Both. The second highest mountain, in the Moka range, climbed from the village of La Laura. The tourism authority says it should only be attempted with the right equipment and a local professional guide.
The Mauritius Glass Gallery, Vacoas-Phoenix. A workshop where one watches craftspeople blow recycled glass and can have a hand print cast in glass.

blocks.text: The east is quieter, with long white beaches, a wide lagoon, small villages and a breeze for most of the year. Trou d'Eau Douce is a fishing village with restaurants along its streets. From this coast boats cross to Ile aux Cerfs.

items: Belle Mare beach. One of the longest beaches on the island. You walk it at sunrise, swim and snorkel, and rest under the casuarinas.
Ile aux Cerfs. An island of 87 hectares off the east coast, reached by boat shuttle from Pointe Maurice. You spend the day on its beaches, try water sports or play its 18-hole golf course.
Central Flacq Market. The largest outdoor market on the island. You shop for produce, souvenirs and clothing and eat street food. All the stalls are open on Wednesdays and Sundays.

Bras d'Eau National Park. A park of 497.2 hectares in the north-east, with a visitor centre, the ruins of an old sugar mill village and a fairly easy trail of 5 km there and back. You walk and watch birds.
Roches Noires lava tubes. A small reserve of volcanic caves. You follow the cave trail down into Princess Margaret Cave and visit the museum.
La Vallée de Ferney. A conservation park of 200 hectares of native forest north of Mahébourg. You hike or cycle its trails, join a guided walk or take a 4x4 tour, and look for the Mauritius kestrel.
Eau Bleue waterfall, Cluny. A waterfall with a pool of blue water, hidden among sugar cane fields. You walk down a slippery path to swim.

blocks.text: The south is wilder: fishing villages, wide beaches, and waves breaking against cliffs of volcanic rock. Inland are tea plantations, old estate houses and the sacred lake of Ganga Talao. Strong currents and reefs mean that not every beach on this coast is for swimming.

items: Blue Bay Marine Park. A marine park of 353 hectares known for its coral garden. You snorkel from Blue Bay beach or take a glass-bottom boat.
Ile aux Aigrettes. A small islet and nature reserve off the south-east coast. You take a guided tour to look for the pink pigeon, the Mauritius fody, tortoises and rare plants.
Frederik Hendrik Museum, Vieux Grand Port. The site of the first Dutch settlement, with French ruins built on the Dutch fort. You walk the ruins and see the finds from the excavations.
National History Museum, Mahébourg. A museum of the island's Dutch, French and British periods in an 18th-century mansion. It has been closed for renovation since 15 December 2025.
Pont Naturel. A natural bridge of volcanic rock over the sea, between Le Souffleur and Le Bouchon. You come to watch the waves. It is not a place to swim.
Gris Gris, Souillac. A beach at the southern tip, with cliffs and heavy surf. You walk, look at the sea and follow the path to La Roche qui Pleure. It is not for swimming.
Rochester Falls. A waterfall about 10 metres high, 2.5 km from Souillac. You swim in the pool and picnic. The tourism authority advises against a visit during or after heavy rain.
Cascade Léon. A waterfall near Souillac, reached by a forest path. You picnic, swim and can swim behind the fall to a cave.
Robert Edward Hart Memorial Museum, Souillac. The poet's house, kept as he lived in it. You see his desk, books and manuscripts.

La Vanille Nature Park, Rivière des Anguilles. A wildlife park known for its Aldabra giant tortoises and Nile crocodiles. You see the tortoises, watch the crocodiles being fed and visit the insectarium and fossil museum.

Ganga Talao, or Grand Bassin. A crater lake that is an important Hindu site, with a statue of Shiva 33 metres high. You walk the shore past the shrines. Pilgrims come on foot from all over the island for Maha Shivaratri.
The Tea Route. Three estates: Domaine des Aubineaux, Bois Chéri and Saint Aubin. You see the tea plantations, visit a tea museum, taste the teas and have lunch in an old colonial house.
Bel Ombre. A quiet coast of white beaches backed by forest, for swimming and snorkelling. Its World of Seashells Museum shows about 8,000 shells.
St Felix beach. A wide, quiet beach between Souillac and Bel Ombre. The water is shallow near the shore but has strong currents, so many come for the sand and beach games.

Vallé Advenature Park. A park of 450 acres with viewpoints over the south coast. You ride a zip line of 1.5 km, cross a suspended bridge, take a quad bike or walk to the waterfalls and the 23-coloured earth.

blocks.text: The west has sunsets, beaches and beach bars, with dolphins offshore. The south-west holds the largest national park, the coloured earth of Chamarel and the mountain of Le Morne Brabant, which can be seen from much of this coast.

items: Black River Gorges National Park. The island's largest national park, 6,574 hectares of forest with some 60 km of trails. You hike, from the easy Savanne Trail to the strenuous Parakeet Trail, and look out over Alexandra Falls from the signposted viewpoint.
Black River Peak. The highest point on the island, at 828 metres, inside the park. The park service lists a moderate trail of 9 km there and back.

Chamarel 7 Coloured Earth Geopark. Sand dunes in seven colours, a park of giant tortoises and two viewpoints over Chamarel Waterfall, the island's tallest. The visit is self-guided and takes 45 minutes to 2 hours.
La Rhumerie de Chamarel. A rum distillery among the cane fields. A guide explains how the rum is made, and the visit ends with a tasting.
Ebony Forest, Chamarel. A conservation project restoring native forest. You walk a raised walkway, take a jeep tour with a guide or join a birdwatching walk.

7 Cascades, or Tamarin Falls. A chain of seven waterfalls reached from Henrietta. You hike down past the falls, the highest of which is 45 metres, and can swim. Guides lead longer routes and canyoning.

Le Morne Brabant mountain trail. The mountain where people who escaped slavery took refuge, a World Heritage Site since 10 July 2008. You climb an easy first section of 2.53 km to a viewpoint, and a steep second section of 760 metres to a metal cross at 492 metres.
Trou Chenille Open Air Museum, Le Morne. A replica of the old village at the foot of the mountain. You visit five huts that show cooking, sega, crafts, fishing and traditional healing.
Le Morne beach. White sand at the foot of the mountain. You learn to kitesurf, as the trade winds are strong from April to November, or stay for the sunset.
La Prairie beach. A beach between Baie du Cap and Le Morne, with shallow water for snorkelling. Seaplane flights take off from here.

The underwater waterfall. An optical illusion off Le Morne, where sand sliding off the ocean shelf looks like a waterfall beneath the sea. It can only be seen properly from the air, by helicopter or seaplane.
Flic en Flac beach. A beach about eight kilometres long. You swim, snorkel, eat at the street food stands and leave from here on diving trips to sites such as the Cathedral.
Casela Nature Parks, Cascavelle. A nature and leisure park of 350 hectares. You go on safari, visit the aviaries and try zip lines, quad bikes and a toboggan run.
Tamarin salt pans. The last working salt pans on the island. You watch salt being harvested with techniques some 200 years old. Go early in the morning to see the workers.
La Preneuse beach. A quiet beach with a Martello tower and old cannons. You walk, watch the sunset and take boat trips from nearby.
Dolphin and whale watching. Bottlenose and spinner dolphins are seen off the west coast, sperm whales all year and humpback whales from July to November. You go out with a licensed operator.
Île aux Bénitiers. An uninhabited island in the lagoon near Le Morne, reached by boat from La Gaulette or Case Noyale. You picnic, watch birds and snorkel to Crystal Rock.
Albion. A quiet village with a beach and a lighthouse 30 metres tall, still in use. You snorkel, walk or cycle the coast and watch the sunset.

blocks.text: Rodrigues is an island dependency of Mauritius, about 580 kilometres away and around an hour and a half by air. It is 18 km long and 8 km at its widest, hilly, and ringed by coral reefs and a wide lagoon. The tourism authority suggests adding 5 to 7 days there to a holiday in Mauritius. Its climate is a little warmer and drier than that of Mauritius, with trade winds all year.

items: François Leguat Reserve, Anse Quitor. A reserve of 20 hectares with hundreds of giant tortoises and a limestone show cave, Grande Caverne. Visits are by guided tour only.
Ile aux Cocos. A small islet nature reserve known for its seabirds, with white sand and coconut trees. You go across by boat.
Trou d'Argent. An isolated beach between two low cliffs, reached only on foot by the coastal path.
The lagoon. You snorkel and dive on the reefs, go line fishing with a local fisherman, and kitesurf in the south-east, where the island hosts an International Kitesurf Festival.
Hiking and cycling. The hills, valleys and coastal paths are good for both, especially on the east coast.
Food and music. You try octopus, sausage rougaille, red bean soup and papaya pie, and watch the Sega Tambour, the traditional dance of Rodrigues.

items: Château de Labourdonnais. The Château is open Monday to Sunday from 9am to 4pm. Access to the estate is free, and there is an entry fee for the Château and for tastings.
Ile aux Cerfs. The leisure island is open every day from 09:00 to 18:00. The boat shuttle from Pointe Maurice runs every 30 minutes from 09:30 to 18:00.
La Vallée de Ferney. Open every day, from 8:30am to 2pm for activities. Access is limited on some dates from June to September. The reserve recommends booking in advance.
Le Morne mountain trail. Open every day, public holidays included, from 9.00 to 16.00. The latest time to start up is 14.30.
Casela Nature Parks. Open every day, public holidays included, from 9am to 5pm. Closed on 25 December and 1 January.
François Leguat Reserve, Rodrigues. Open every day from 09h00 to 17h00, by guided tour only, at 9:30, 10:30, 13:30 and 14:30.

Le Morne. The trail closes for heavy or torrential rain warnings, from cyclone warning Class II, and after landslides or rockfalls. Sign the visitor book at the trailhead. A liability form is required for the second section, which children under 13 should not climb. A qualified guide is recommended for it.
Boats. Go with an operator licensed by the Tourism Authority. A commercial boat has a registration number beginning with PC. Wear the lifejacket provided.
Dolphins. Under the regulations of 2012, boats approach from the side at no-wake speed. Nobody may feed or touch a dolphin, and no more than three swimmers may be in the water at once.
Diving. Diving centres are overseen by the Mauritius Scuba Diving Association, which publishes a list of approved centres.
Beaches. All beaches are public. On the south coast, mind the currents and reefs.
Hikes. Wear proper shoes, take sunscreen and plenty of water, and tell someone where you are going. A local, certified guide is recommended.
Casela. On 20 November 2026 the park's site said animal feeding was suspended as a precaution against foot-and-mouth disease. The park was open.

unverified: Prices, tour times and booking for Ile aux Aigrettes. The Mauritian Wildlife Foundation website could not be reached on 20 November 2026.
The UNESCO World Heritage pages for Le Morne and Aapravasi Ghat. They returned a verification screen. Inscription dates are those given by the two trust funds.

Entry fees for the Château de Labourdonnais, Eureka House, Casela, Ile aux Cerfs, the François Leguat Reserve, La Vallée de Ferney, the World of Seashells Museum and the Roches Noires lava tubes. None was stated clearly on a page that was read.

Opening hours for Eureka House, La Citadel, Kwan Tee Pagoda, Maheswarnath Mandir, the two markets, the World of Seashells Museum, the lava tubes, Trou Chenille Open Air Museum, Vallé Advenature Park and the Tea Route estates.
Whether the National History Museum in Mahébourg has reopened. The Museums Council's page still showed it closed for renovation.
Ebony Forest's own site. It was read through a summarising fetch only, so its tour times and prices were left out of this guide.

Figures on which official and tourism pages disagree: the length of Belle Mare beach, the length of trails in Black River Gorges, the size of the Chamarel geopark, the number of species at Odysseo and the number of holes on the Ile aux Cerfs golf course. Where a figure is given, it is the one from the place's own or the official page.
Whether 7 Cascades lies inside Black River Gorges National Park, as the tourism authority's waterfalls page says, and whether a guide or permit is needed there or on Le Pouce.
The village where Vallé Advenature Park stands. Neither the park's page nor the tourism authority's page read gives it.

Rodrigues. The Rodrigues tourism website could not be reached, so that section rests on the tourism promotion authority's page and the François Leguat Reserve's own site. The tourism page calls the Sega Tambour a UNESCO World Heritage, which could not be checked on a UNESCO page.
The Intercontinental Slavery Museum in Port Louis. Its official site gives no visiting hours, so it was left out.
Whether a fee is charged to climb Le Morne. The Trust's visitor leaflet mentions none.
Guide rates at the Pamplemousses garden. The Trust's services page shows two different scales, so no figure is given here.
